name: Steam Engine as GPT
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Machine That Taught Economies What General Purpose Means
lesson.summary: The steam engine took roughly a century to go from a narrow mine pumping device to a true general purpose technology, illustrating how long real transformation can take even for an eventual success.
lesson.body:
A General Purpose Technology, or GPT, is an economic category, unrelated to the modern generative pretrained transformer language models that happen to share the same acronym, developed by economists trying to explain why a small number of historical technologies drove outsized, broad, and durable economic growth while most inventions, however clever, stayed narrow. The three defining tests, covered in earlier chapters, are that a true GPT must be broadly applicable across many sectors, must keep improving substantially over time rather than arriving fully formed, and must enable a wave of complementary innovation that would not have been possible without it.

The steam engine's real history shows what clearing those tests actually looks like, and how long it can take. Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine of 1712 was narrow, useful mainly for pumping water out of flooded coal mines, and quite inefficient. James Watt's improvements starting in the 1760s and 1770s, especially the separate condenser, dramatically raised efficiency and, crucially, made rotary motion practical rather than just up and down pumping motion, which is what actually opened the door to broad applicability.

Test one, broad applicability: once practical rotary steam power existed, it spread across textile mills, flour and paper mills, mining operations, and eventually railways and steamships, industries with essentially nothing in common except a shared need for reliable mechanical power that did not depend on water flow, wind, or animal and human muscle.

Test two, improvement over time: steam engine efficiency and power density improved substantially across the nineteenth century through higher operating pressures, compound and later triple expansion designs, and better materials, and each generation of improvement opened applications, like practical steam locomotion and transoceanic steamships, that earlier, weaker engines simply could not have supported.

Test three, enabling further innovation: the steam engine did not just replace existing sources of mechanical power. It enabled the concentration of production in the factory system, made railways and their enormous downstream effects on markets, land use, and even standardized time possible, and helped make steam powered shipping and, eventually, steam turbines for early electricity generation possible, a chain of complementary innovation that runs for well over a century.

The pattern worth carrying forward is the lag: the steam engine took roughly a century, from Newcomen's narrow pumping engine to a genuinely economy transforming general purpose technology, moving through its own long, unglamorous engineering improvement phase, exactly the kind of gap the Science vs Engineering Gap chapter describes, well before its broadest effects arrived. That long stretch between initial demonstration and broad transformative impact is worth holding onto as this book turns, later, to asking the same three questions of quantum computing.
